title: Fred Warner has turned the Peanut Punch into a 49ers defensive staple
text:
Fred Warner has turned the Peanut Punch into a 49ers defensive staple Schedule NFL News Draft Fantasy Odds Betting Newsletter NINERS Fred Warner has turned the Peanut Punch into a 49ers defensive staple
 Oliver G. Niners Wire Nov. 6, 2026, 5:01 p.m. PT Fred Warner has become one of the NFL's most effective players at punching the football out, and the San Francisco 49ers linebacker is making sure the rest of the defense follows his lead.
 The technique, known as the "Peanut Punch," is named after former Chicago Bears cornerback Charles "Peanut" Tillman, who popularized punching the football out of ball carriers during his NFL career. What Tillman helped make famous has become a staple of Warner's game, and now he's trying to make it part of San Francisco's defensive identity.
 Warner is tied for the NFL lead with four forced fumbles through seven games this season, matching his career high. He has 21 forced fumbles over his career, including 14 in his last 43 games.
 His impact extends beyond his own production. According to The Athletic's Vic Tafur , the 49ers have made forcing fumbles a priority under head coach Kyle Shanahan and new defensive coordinator Raheem Morris, even maintaining a punch-out leaderboard during training camp. Warner has effectively made it a competition for second place.
 Rookie linebacker Jaden Dugger is among those embracing the technique. After nearly punching the ball loose against Seattle in Week 5, Dugger explained how much Warner's example has influenced him.

"It was emphasized so much at camp that now it's just an instinct," Dugger said. "Fred perfected it, so I just watch him. And he's always telling me to punch through the ball."
 Warner's influence is particularly notable considering he wasn't always successful with the technique himself. Early in his career, he struggled to balance punching the football with making the tackle. Former 49ers linebackers coach and defensive coordinator DeMeco Ryans (who is now the head coach for the Houston Texans) eventually told him to stop attempting it altogether.
 Warner listened for about 10 days, according to Tafur, before punching the ball out of Germain Ifedi's hands against the Seattle Seahawks in 2019, setting up a DeForest Buckner fumble recovery touchdown.
 "Sometimes you gotta overcome coaching in those moments, right?" Warner joked.
 Now, Warner wants the technique to become second nature for everyone in San Francisco's defense.
 "My job is to create an infectious type of energy," Warner told Tafur. "Like, 'Man, this is just what we do — we all attack the football.'"
 With Warner continuing to produce takeaways and younger players adopting his approach, the 49ers are building a defensive identity around one of their captain's greatest strengths.
